na buddher avabodho 'sti nātmano vidyate kriyā /
ato nānyatarasyāpi jānātīti ca yujyate //
passages.literal_translation: The appearance of the self is what the finite verb ending expresses, and the root-meaning is the intellect’s activity. Both, through non-discrimination, are falsely spoken of as “knows.” There is no awareness belonging to the intellect, and no activity exists in the self. Therefore “knows” is not appropriate to either one [by itself].

passages.literal_translation: People accept a likeness of the face in a mirror, for the face’s reflection is seen in the form of the face. Where there is the appearance of one in another, through non-discrimination of just those two, all people naturally speak of the activity as “knows.” Having superimposed the intellect’s agency, the knower is said to know; likewise, having superimposed consciousness, knowingness is here spoken of as belonging to the intellect. Knowledge is the self’s own nature, eternal light, because of scripture; therefore it is never made by the intellect, by the self, or by another.

passages.literal_translation: The shadow’s conformity to the mirror is cast upon the face; in the same way, conformity to the intellect’s properties is accepted of the appearance of awareness. Therefore the intellect’s cognitions, illuminated by the appearance of the self, appear as though apprehenders, just as firebrands and the like appear as though burning.

passages.literal_translation: If it is thought that establishment would occur near the witness: no, because nothing is contributed to the witness, and because the consequence would extend elsewhere. [Objection:] Surely thus there would be a transfer of seeing, like fire into an iron ball? [Reply:] This has been ruled out by saying “like the appearance of a face in a mirror.” Black iron with a red appearance is stated as what is observed; the example and the illustrated case are nowhere alike in every respect.

passages.literal_translation: In statements such as “you are that,” because the meaning of “you” has not been discriminated, the sentence-meaning “I am eternally free” is not manifested. The statement of agreement and difference is for that discrimination, not otherwise. For when the meaning of “you” has been discriminated, as a bilva fruit placed in the hand, the sentence-meaning thus becomes manifest, solely from the meaning of “I,” through exclusion of “afflicted” and through determination of the inward self.

passages.literal_translation: Knowledge of eternal freedom comes from the sentence, not otherwise; knowledge of the sentence-meaning also has recollection of word-meanings as its antecedent. Through agreement and difference the word-meaning is certainly recalled; thus one understands the self as free of affliction and inactive. From statements such as “Being alone,” knowledge concerning the inward self would become clearer, just as from “you are the tenth.”

passages.literal_translation: In “you are that,” the word “are” would mean that “that” and “you” have the same abode [referent]. The word “that” has the inward self as its meaning, and “you” likewise has the meaning of “that.” Both should ward off affliction and non-inward-selfhood; thus they should mutually convey the meaning of “not this, not this.”

passages.literal_translation: For the self is not adventitious to anyone, being established by itself. For the self is not established by awaiting a means of knowledge about itself. Its means of knowledge, perception and the others, are employed to establish objects of knowledge not already established. For no one accepts things such as space as established by themselves independently of means of knowledge. The self, however, because it is the support of transactions involving means of knowledge and the rest, is established before those transactions. Nor is negation of such [a self] possible. An adventitious thing is negated, not one’s own nature. For whoever is the negator is precisely that one’s own nature. Fire’s heat is not negated by fire.

passages.literal_translation: [Objection:] If Brahman is not an object, its having scripture as source is untenable. [Reply:] No, because scripture has as its aim the cessation of difference imagined through ignorance. For scripture does not intend to communicate Brahman as an object in the manner “this.”

passages.literal_translation: [Objection:] Even while the capacity for agency remains, the human goal will be accomplished through avoiding agency’s effect; and avoiding that [effect] comes from avoiding its occasion, just as fire, though endowed with the capacity to burn, has no burning-effect through separation from wood. [Reply:] No, because it is impossible wholly to avoid even the occasions, connected through the relation characterized by capacity. [Objection:] Liberation will be accomplished because its means are prescribed. [Reply:] No, because what depends on means is impermanent. Moreover, liberation is held to be established through teaching the self as eternally pure, aware and free. Teaching such a self would not be possible if agency were intrinsic. Therefore the self’s agency is only through superimposition of properties of limiting conditions, not intrinsic.

passages.literal_translation: Nor is the seeing that is seen capable of making the seer an object, so that one might desire it. Nor is there a desire on the part of oneself concerning one’s own nature as an object. Therefore “it knew only itself” means solely the cessation of superimposition through ignorance, not making the self an object.

passages.literal_translation: That is complete, pervasive like space, without gaps and without limiting conditions. This very [reality], with limiting conditions, situated in name and form, entered into transactions, is complete—pervasive through its own nature as the supreme Self, not through its particular nature delimited by limiting conditions. This Brahman, entered into particularity and having the nature of an effect, rises from the complete having the nature of a cause: rises up, comes forth—this is the meaning. Although it rises as an effect, it does not abandon what is its own nature, completeness, the condition of the supreme Self; it comes forth complete.

passages.literal_translation: Here some explain: the complete effect rises from the complete cause. The arisen effect is complete even while present, a thing that is ultimately real in the form of duality. Again, at dissolution, taking the completeness of the complete effect and placing it in oneself, the complete alone remains as cause. Thus in all three times—origination, continuance and dissolution—cause and effect are complete. That completeness is one, designated through the distinction of cause and effect. Thus Brahman is one, with the nature of duality and nonduality. Just as, supposedly, the ocean consists precisely of water, waves, foam, bubbles and the rest; and just as water is real and its arising waves, foam, bubbles and the rest are the ocean itself, possess appearance and disappearance, and are ultimately real: so all this duality is ultimately real, occupying the place of waves and the rest, while highest Brahman occupies the place of the ocean’s water.

passages.literal_translation: But here, concerning reality, no option is possible of “it may be duality or it may be nonduality,” because the reality that is the self is not dependent on a person; and because duality and nonduality in one thing contradict. Therefore this conception has not been carefully intended. [Objection:] If Brahman has the nature of duality and nonduality, there are examples such as the ocean; how do you say that duality and nonduality of one thing contradict? [Reply:] No, because [those examples] concern another domain. We said that duality and nonduality contradict concerning an eternal, partless reality, not concerning a composite effect.

passages.literal_translation: The course of the restrained, nonconceptual mind of the discerning person is to be understood; in deep sleep it is different, not the same as that. For in deep sleep it subsides; restrained, it does not subside. That very [reality] is fearless Brahman, the light of knowledge all around. Unborn, sleepless, dreamless, nameless, formless, once-for-all manifest, all-knowing: this is in no way a figurative expression.

passages.literal_translation: In subsidence one should awaken the mind; when distracted, quiet it again. One should recognize it as having residual coloring; when it has reached evenness, one should not stir it. One should not savor happiness there; one should become unattached through discernment. One should effortfully unify the mind when, though still, it goes outward. When the mind neither subsides nor is distracted again, then that, unmoving and without appearance, is accomplished Brahman.

No jīva whatsoever is born; its coming-to-be does not exist. This is that highest truth in which nothing whatsoever is born.

passages.literal_translation: But if, when [reality] has been understood from another sentence directed at reality, the prescribing of a stream of cognitions concerning it is desired, let it be: there is no fault. And thus “having understood, one should develop understanding” shows that knowledge of the self’s reality is established. Or that too is useless, because its object is already obtained. For repeated contemplation of that has immediate realization as its result, an observed purpose; no result other than that is sought. For immortality is not different from the manifestation of one’s own nature, as explained before.

passages.literal_translation: This is the intention: we do not declare ignorance to be one in all jīvas like pradhāna, so that we would be reproached in this way; rather it differs for each jīva. Therefore ignorance is removed only for the jīva for whom knowledge has arisen, not for another jīva, because knowledge and ignorance in different loci do not contradict. Whence, then, the consequence that all saṃsāra would be destroyed?

passages.literal_translation: The jīva is not other than the self. Nor is it a modification of that; rather it is the self itself with a delimitation imagined through the condition of ignorance. As space with a delimitation imagined through a pot or jar is pot-space or jar-space, it is not other than supreme space or a modification of it.

passages.literal_translation: The intention is this: true, immediate realization of Brahman is not directly the result of scripture and reasoning; rather the mind itself, assisted by dispositions laid down by knowledge of the meaning of reasoning and scripture, establishes in Brahman an intellect-modification possessing immediate realization.

passages.literal_translation: Even though [the self] is partless, with the varied manifold superimposed by beginningless indeterminable ignorance and its dispositions, [it is] as though possessing parts; through nonapprehension of some part, [there is] as though error. Ultimately, however, there is no so-called error and no so-called saṃsāra.

passages.literal_translation: “The prototype-consciousness conditioned by ignorance is Īśvara; consciousness reflected in ignorance delimited by the inner instrument and its dispositions is jīva”: thus the authors of the Vivaraṇa. “Consciousness reflected in ignorance is Īśvara; consciousness reflected in intellect is jīva; prototype-consciousness conditioned by ignorance is pure”: thus the author of the Saṃkṣepaśārīraka. In these two positions the plurality of jīvas follows from difference of intellects. “Consciousness made the object of ignorance is Īśvara, and made its locus is jīva”: thus Vācaspati Miśra. In this position plurality of jīvas follows from plurality of ignorance.

śrutitātparyaviṣayībhūtārthaviruddhatvaṃ ca heyam eveti śataśa udghoṣitam asmābhiḥ /
passages.literal_translation: For the nondual reality of the self is scripture’s principal object of knowledge, because it is fruitful and unknown. Conceptions such as division into jīva and Īśvara, although arising merely from human understanding, are restated by scripture because they are useful for knowledge of reality: according to the rule that what is without its own fruit, in proximity to what has a fruit, is subordinate to it, and because scripture can restate even what is established through error. We have proclaimed hundreds of times that contradiction of the meaning intended by scripture must indeed be rejected.

ekatvasaṅkhyāyogi ekam / tad apekṣābuddhijanyadvitvasaṅkhyāyogi dvitīyam / tata ekābhāve dvitīyaṃ kutaḥ syāt / dvitīyaṃ ca tṛtīyādīnām apy upalakṣaṇam / nanu, "ekam evādvitīyam" (chu vi.2.1.) iti śrutyā ekatvaṃ pratipādyate / na, ity āha -- na vā kevalatvam iti / kevalam ekatvaṃ, tasyāvidyakatvāt / yady ātmana ekatvaṃ śrutyā na pratipādyate, tarhi pratyakṣādipramāṇavaśād anekatvaṃ syād iti cet, na, ity āha -- na cākevalatvam iti / akevalatvam anekatvaṃ, "neha nānāsti kiñcana" (bau iv.4.19.), "ekam evādvitīyam" (chu vi.2.1.), "athāta ādeśo neti neti" (bau ii.3.6.) ityādiśrutibhyaḥ /

passages.literal_translation: “One” is what possesses the number one. “Second” is what possesses the number two generated by a cognition of reference to that [one]. Therefore, when there is no one, whence a second? “Second” also stands for third and the rest. [Objection:] Scripture, “one alone, without a second,” teaches oneness. [Reply:] No; he says “nor sole-ness.” Sole-ness is oneness, because that is due to ignorance. [Objection:] If the self’s oneness is not taught by scripture, plurality would follow through perception and other means of knowledge. [Reply:] No; he says “nor non-sole-ness.” Non-sole-ness is plurality, [excluded] by scriptural passages including “there is no plurality here whatsoever,” “one alone, without a second,” and “not this, not this.” He gives the reason throughout: “because of nonduality.” What has gone twofold is dvīta; its condition is duality. The Vārttika says: “They call what has gone twofold dvīta; its condition is called duality.” Where duality, the condition of being twofold, does not exist, that is advaita: this is the literal meaning, because scripture says “one seer like water, nondual.”

passages.literal_translation: Or else the particular ignorance-states of root ignorance itself are the coverings of objects such as pots. Because ignorance occupies the place of prior absence, it is accepted that there are as many ignorances as knowledges; and because one knowledge destroys only one ignorance, even when a pot-cognition destroys covering there is no inconsistency.

passages.literal_translation: First, the extraordinary knowledge “I am Brahman” arises from sentences such as “you are that,” immediately upon hearing. Nor does a means of knowledge concerning an established supersensible reality await an inferential mark or the like, or a means of knowledge consisting in yogic perception, because [that reality] is not their object. The meaning understood from sentences such as “not this” and “not gross” is not accessible to yogic perception, because it is inward.

passages.literal_translation: Here understanding not dependent on another is called nididhyāsana; its introduction is intended as the culmination of the preceding two. The activity of hearing and the rest must be performed here with effort until the knowledge described becomes luminously manifest. “Through knowledge” is said to remove the suspicion of meditation, because meditation is suspected from the word nididhyāsana. I previously stated that meditation and the rest cause the arising of knowledge; knowledge itself is for its own purpose, remembered as having liberation alone as its fruit.

passages.literal_translation: In the inward self, however, self-manifest because its nature is consciousness, the nonappearance of Brahman-nature, having no other occasion, occurs only through obstruction by the naturally established ignorance-power there. Therefore it obstructs the appearance of Brahman-nature in inward consciousness and is an occasion of the appearance of ego and the rest which do not have that nature.

passages.literal_translation: If a transformation of the shell into silver-form occasioned by a defect is asserted, this too is without substance. For in curd, the transformation of milk, cancellation “this is not curd” is not seen; nor the cognition “this is milk.” Here, however, both are seen. Moreover, if the shell transformed into silver-form like milk into curd-form, even upon disappearance of the defect it would remain just so.

passages.literal_translation: [Objection:] How, when the lump of clay, the cause, is known, would another thing, the effect, be known? [Reply:] This is no fault, because the effect is not other than the cause. You think that when one thing is known another is not known. That would indeed be so if the effect were other than the cause; but the effect is not thus other than the cause. [Objection:] How then [does one say] in the world, “this is the cause; this is its modification”? [Reply:] Listen. “Having speech as commencement” means having speech as commencement, having speech as support. What is that modification? A name: nāmadheya is simply nāman, the suffix dheya being in its own meaning. It is only a name supported by speech; there is no thing called modification ultimately. Clay alone, clay alone—clay alone exists as the real thing.

passages.literal_translation: Because the word “apprehended” indicates being the counterpositive of absolute absence in that [locus] in precisely the form in which it is apprehended as the locus of that [thing]. That form is a particular relation and a particular delimiter. For the ground’s being the locus of a pot is not apprehended without a particular relation, nor the tree’s being the locus of contact with a monkey without a particular delimiter. Thus, when the definition comes to this—its falsity is being the counterpositive of absolute absence located there through precisely that particular relation and precisely that particular delimiter through which the cognition of that locushood can occur there—where is the proving of what is already established?

passages.literal_translation: Nor should it be said that, since being and absence do not oppose, their cognitions would not stand as cancelled and cancelling: although [being and absence] of different orders of reality do not oppose, those of the same order oppose. For the rule is: on the ground where the absolute absence of a particular pot is transactional, that pot is not transactional there.

This certainly does not belong to shell-silver or the manifold before cancellation; therefore utter nonexistence does not follow.

passages.literal_translation: No, because devotion and Brahman-knowledge differ in nature, means, fruit and qualified recipient. Devotion is the mind’s taking the form of the Lord, preceded by melting, in the form of a determinate modification. Brahman-knowledge is a nondeterminate mental modification, without melting, whose domain is solely the nondual self. Hearing works that arrange the greatness of the Lord’s qualities is the means of devotion. A great Vedānta sentence such as “you are that” is the means of Brahman-knowledge. Intensification of love directed to the Lord is devotion’s fruit; cessation of ignorance, the root of all misfortune, is Brahman-knowledge’s fruit.

passages.literal_translation: Even devotion born of pure sattva is thus [of both fruits] in practitioners such as ourselves; but in accomplished ones such as Sanaka it has only the seen fruit. Devotion has seen and unseen fruits, because of manifestation of happiness and also prescription, like bathing in the Ganges for one whose body is tormented by summer heat. In one overcome by rajas and tamas, the seen portion is obstructed, as for one afflicted by cold wind; the unseen portion is not lost. In the same way, for those liberated while living there is no unseen portion, as for those who, having bathed and eaten, play again in the Ganges. The fruit attainable in the present body is called seen; that to be enjoyed in a future body is called unseen.

passages.literal_translation: [Objection:] From the introduction of examples such as clay, Brahman possessing transformation is understood to be intended by scripture; for things such as clay are known in the world as transforming. [Reply:] No: Brahman’s invariance is understood from scriptural denials of all modification, such as “this great unborn self, unaging, deathless, immortal, fearless, Brahman,” “this self is not this, not this,” and “not gross, not minute.” For transformation and its absence cannot be understood of the one Brahman.

Thus the Lord’s lordship, omniscience and omnipotence depend precisely on delimitation by ignorance-natured limiting conditions; ultimately, in the self whose nature is stripped of every limiting condition by knowledge, transactions of ruler and ruled, omniscience and the rest do not fit.

passages.literal_translation: Here it is said: waking cognitions cannot be like dream cognitions. Why? Because of difference. There is indeed a difference between dream and waking. What difference? We say: cancellation and non-cancellation. For what is apprehended in dream is cancelled for the awakened person: “I falsely apprehended a gathering of many people; there is no such gathering for me; my mind was attached to sleep, and so this error arose.” Likewise in magic and the rest cancellation occurs as appropriate. A thing apprehended in waking, such as a post, is not cancelled in any state in this way.

passages.literal_translation: There is no weakening of knowledge once it has arisen, because there is no cancelling means of knowledge and no cause for the re-arising of ignorance that has ceased. Exhaustion of dispositions and dissolution of mind, however, because firm practice is absent and because they are obstructed from time to time by already-begun karma that gives experience, suddenly cease like a lamp in a windy place.

passages.literal_translation: This fifth stage is devotion’s own nature. From its particular maturation the other six stages are fruits. Then comes realization of one’s own nature: immediate realization of the inward self’s nature as distinct from the pair of gross and subtle bodies is the sixth stage. Otherwise, through distraction by body, senses and the rest, even affection that has arisen could not be sustained.

passages.literal_translation:
The substance of the internal organ, transforming in the form of a succession of modifications like a succession of lamp flames, is called mind because its nature is thinking. Its dissolution means transformation in the form of restraint, having abandoned transformation in the form of modifications.

A disposition is the impression in the mind that causes a particular modification such as anger to arise suddenly without consideration of what precedes and follows, because it has been instilled in the mind through repeated earlier practice. Exhaustion of that disposition means the nonarising of anger and the like even when an external occasion is present, once the pure disposition of tranquility, restraint and the like, born of discrimination, is firm.

passages.literal_translation: In whatever awareness of an object has the form of apprehension or recollection, the self shines directly. For objects do not shine when the object-manifesting self is not manifest. Every awareness arises thus: “I know this”; no cognition arises merely as “knows.”

Just as a goer, though possessing the conjunction that results from going, has no objecthood but only agency, so too the knower should be understood.

passages.literal_translation: The real is endowed with arising, passing away and permanence. […] Arising is the attainment of another condition, through both kinds of conditions, by a conscious or unconscious substance without abandoning its own kind—as a lump of clay attains the pot-mode. Likewise, passing away is departure of the preceding condition, as [the loss] of lump-shape when a pot arises. What persists, becomes stable, through absence of loss or arising in its beginningless constitutive nature is enduring; endurance is its condition or activity—as clay continues through lump, pot and other states.

passages.literal_translation: What has been said is this: arising and the rest are characteristics of substance; substance is what is characterized. Here, relative to the standpoint directed at modes, there is distinctness from one another and from substance. Relative to the standpoint directed at substance, there is nondistinctness, because they are not apprehended separately. Thus the relation of characterized and characteristic is established.

passages.literal_translation: The thing formerly seen is recognized as “this is that very thing” because it occurs again with precisely that nature. If there were complete destruction, or only an entirely new appearance, recollection would not be possible; worldly transactions dependent on it would be contradicted. […] But that [eternity] is to be understood in a qualified way. With eternity in every respect, because there would be no becoming otherwise, the causal process of transmigration and its cessation would be contradicted.

passages.literal_translation: Perfect knowledge [arises] from the destruction of delusion and from the destruction of the knowledge- and perception-obscuring and obstructive [karmas]. […] True [that a shorter wording was possible]; but the formulation in separate clauses is made to teach the order of destruction. Having first brought delusion to destruction, and having obtained the designation “passions destroyed” for less than a muhūrta, one then destroys together the knowledge- and perception-obscuring and obstructive [karmas] and attains perfect knowledge. Their destruction is the cause of perfect knowledge’s arising; therefore the case ending indicating a cause was employed.

passages.literal_translation: Liberation is complete release from all karma, through absence of the causes of bondage and through shedding [karma]. […] [Pūjyapāda:] This rule [of cessation] applies to whatever is other than perfect rightness, knowledge, perception and the state of a perfected being. [Objection:] If only four remain, would not unlimited power and so forth cease? [Reply:] This is no fault: unlimited power and so forth are not separate [exceptions], because they are inseparable from knowledge and perception; for the activity of unlimited cognition is absent in one lacking unlimited capacity, and happiness consists of knowledge.

passages.literal_translation: [Objection:] These released ones have only discourse about past differences, since the causes of differences of destination, birth-class and so forth are absent. [Reply:] There is also difference in a certain respect. Why? […] As regards time: at what time is perfection? With reference to the standpoint of the present, one attaining perfection in a single instant becomes perfected. With reference to the standpoint that describes the past, as regards birth, without further specification, one born in an ascending or descending [time-cycle] attains perfection.

passages.literal_translation: By the two qualifications “agent” and “experiencer” he attacks the Sāṅkhya view: the emphatic construction is “being an agent, he is also an experiencer,” since experience is impossible for a nonagent, and only one able to perform the act of experiencing is an experiencer. [Objection:] Just as redness and so on are predicated of crystal through the proximity of a hibiscus flower and the like, pleasure, pain and other experience may properly be predicated of an inactive [self] through the adjunct of primordial nature. For the person, merely by proximity, is called the enjoyer of objects consisting of pleasure, pain and so forth that have entered the mirror-like intellect, a transformation of primordial nature; as it is said, “The person is conscious of the object determined by intellect.” [Reply:] No. Without activity in some respect, becoming otherwise would be impossible even with primordial nature as an adjunct. What has not departed from its earlier form is not fit for that predication; if it does depart, activity follows from abandoning the earlier form and assuming the later. Even in the crystal example, redness that fails to appear in an opaque stone and the like through the hibiscus flower’s proximity, but does appear there [in the crystal], indicates such a transformation of it. […] Thus being an experiencer does not fit the inactive.

For: even the one who is free of “mine” and “I” is not found. Whoever sees one free of “mine” and “I” does not see.

passages.literal_translation: Liberation comes from the ending of action and afflictions; action and afflictions arise from conceptual construction; those [constructions] from proliferation, while proliferation ceases in emptiness. […] From the departure of proliferation comes cessation of conceptual construction; from cessation of conceptual construction, cessation of all action and afflictions; and from cessation of action and afflictions, cessation of birth.

passages.literal_translation: [Nāgārjuna:] “Self” has also been designated, and “nonself” also taught; the Buddhas have also taught that there is neither any self nor any nonself. […] [Candrakīrti:] To turn away from unwholesomeness and so forth those less advanced pupils who perform unwholesome actions, the Blessed Buddhas in some cases also designated “self,” establishing it in the world. […] For those intermediate pupils, to loosen fixation on the view of a real personal identity and to generate desire for nirvāṇa, […] “nonself” too was taught. […] For those advanced pupils whose attachment to self has gone […] [the neither-self-nor-nonself teaching quoted again in the intervening text]. […] For just as the view of self is not reality, so the view of nonself that opposes it is itself not reality.

passages.literal_translation: What is dependent arising, that we declare to be emptiness. That is designation in dependence [on something]; that itself is the middle way. This dependent arising—the appearance of sprouts, cognitions and so forth depending upon causes and conditions—is nonarising by intrinsic nature. And the nonarising of things by intrinsic nature is emptiness.

passages.literal_translation: Likewise, for yogins superior to us, in atoms, released selves and minds that are alike in shape, qualities and action—that is, alike in shape, alike in qualities, alike in actions—those grounds from which, no other ground being possible, there arises for each substrate the discriminating cognition “this is distinct from that,” are ultimate particularizers.

Yet neither of them is simply nonexistent then, because they are recognized on awakening. […] But the existence of manifestation when it is not manifest is not accepted.

passages.literal_translation: From this it should be understood that, in sections concerning the individual self, the intention of scriptural declarations of unity of self is precisely discrimination, through nondifference characterized by absence of dissimilarity; for discriminative knowledge alone is said to cause liberation as correct knowledge. But a section concerning the supreme Self should be understood to intend the selfhood of the supreme Self alone, through discrimination even from the individual self.

And because Brahman’s selfhood itself, owing to its preeminence, is the general meaning in all the Vedānta texts.

passages.literal_translation: The disposition arising from the wisdom of concentration counters the accumulated dispositions of emergence [from concentration]. Because the dispositions of emergence are overpowered, the cognitions produced by them do not occur. […] [Objection:] How will this increase of dispositions not give the mind an ongoing function? [Reply:] Those dispositions produced by wisdom do not endow the mind with an ongoing function, because they cause the exhaustion of afflictions. For they bring the mind to an end with respect to its own work: the activity of mind culminates in discernment.

passages.literal_translation: [Objection:] Granted that dispassion, being a cognition, counters wisdom, which is cognitive; but how does it counter a disposition that is not a cognition? […] [Reply:] The meaning is that the wisdom-disposition is countered precisely by a disposition born of the higher dispassion cultivated for a long time, uninterruptedly and with care—not by cognition. […] And in the cessation of every modification there is no perception for the yogin, nor memory.

passages.literal_translation: Therefore those dispositions oppose the mind’s ongoing function; they are not causes of its persistence. Since the mind, its function completed, ceases together with the dispositions conducive to isolation, when it has ceased, the person is established in nothing but its own nature; hence it is called pure, isolated and liberated.

passages.literal_translation: Thus, having stated discriminative contemplation as the means of stopping emergence [from concentration], the sūtra-author states the means of stopping discriminative contemplation. […] This is what is said: dispassionate toward discriminative contemplation and wishing its cessation, one should cultivate the concentration called “cloud of dharma.” Through cultivating it, discriminative discernment occurs in every respect. And thereby one becomes capable of stopping it.

passages.literal_translation: [Objection:] Granted that the highest limit of the cloud of dharma—higher dispassion consisting solely of clarity of knowledge—destroys at their roots the dispositions of emergence and concentration and the deposits of affliction and karma; but the qualities by themselves are disposed to produce transformations. Why do they not initiate bodies, senses and so forth even for such a person? Therefore [the sūtra-author] says [4.32]. […] The meaning is: this is the disposition of the qualities, that they do not operate for the one for whom their purpose has been fulfilled.

[…] [Vācaspati:] For consciousness-power is established in its own nature even during great dissolution; yet that is not liberation. Therefore [the commentator] says “as for.”

passages.literal_translation: But in truth there is just one transformation. For a property is nothing but the form of its bearer; this is precisely the bearer’s modification, elaborated through its properties. In this case, the property, while existing in its bearer, undergoes a change of condition across the past, future and present courses, but not a change of substance. Thus, when a gold vessel is broken and made otherwise, there is a change of condition, but no change of the gold.

passages.literal_translation: Here is an example. The clay bearer, passing from the property of lump-form to another property, transforms with respect to property: it is pot-form. Pot-form leaves the future temporal mark and takes on the present temporal mark: it transforms with respect to temporal mark. The pot, undergoing newness and oldness at every moment, takes on transformation of condition. A further property is also a condition of the bearer, and a further temporal mark is a condition of the property. Thus one transformation of substance is displayed through distinctions. This is to be applied to other things as well.

passages.literal_translation: But for one for whom this is merely properties without a continuing connection, there is no experience [of the result]. Why? How can a different cognition be entitled as experiencer of an action done by another cognition? Nor would there be memory of it: one does not remember what another has seen. And because of recognition of an object, a persisting, continuing bearer is established: what has undergone alteration of property is recognized. Therefore this is not merely properties without a continuing connection.

passages.literal_translation: And this permanence is twofold: immutable permanence and permanence through transformation. Of these, immutable permanence belongs to the conscious subject; permanence through transformation belongs to the guṇas. That is permanent whose reality is not destroyed while it transforms; both are permanent because the reality of each is undestroyed.

passages.literal_translation: Objection: Since difference between the individual and Brahman has been stated, how could the individual have the cognition “I am Brahman”? Reply: Just as, in the Sāṅkhya account, the individual, although different from the inner organ, is the object of that organ’s valid cognition “I” through being its self, so Brahman, although different from [things] beginning with the individual and ending with the body, could be the object of the inner organ’s valid cognition “I” through being the self of the individual and the rest. For it has been stated that Brahman alone is the ultimate self of all, through being the inner ruler and the support into which the individual and the rest dissolve. And just as ignorance in the form of identification with the body ceases through knowing the individual as self, so identification with the individual and the rest would cease through knowing Brahman as self.

passages.literal_translation: Objection: How can difference and nondifference, being opposed, occur together in one [place]? [Reply:] Because difference characterized as mutual absence does not conflict with nondifference characterized as nondivision. And even difference and nondifference in the forms of division and nondivision do not conflict when time differs, and when practical and ultimate [standpoints] differ.

passages.literal_translation: As for “thus”: the practice of those twenty-five principles, beginning with the conscious subject and ending with the elements, is practice of the principles. It is precisely through practice that there is vision of the principles. From that practice cognition arises for the conscious subject: “I am not the principles; the principles are not mine; I do not belong to the principles. Rather, these belong to primordial nature.” Therefore knowledge arises, and so on. “Remainderless” means without remainder. What else? [The witness adds parenthetically: “knowledge, since he says”:] “from non-error.” Error is doubt; its opposite is non-error. From that non-error, from absence of doubt, from seeing the object as it actually is, pure—that is, faultless—unmixed, isolated knowledge arises, becomes manifest. What knowledge? [Knowledge] whose form is apprehending the difference between the guṇas and the conscious subject: this is the meaning.

passages.literal_translation: The mind is colored by the object to be thought. And since it is itself an object, it is connected with the conscious subject which has it as object, through a vṛtti belonging to that subject [the possessive is read here with Vācaspati’s explanation below]. This very mind, colored by seer and seen, presenting object and subject, having taken on the forms of conscious and unconscious, though of the nature of an object appearing as if not an object, and though unconscious appearing as if conscious, is called “having every object,” like a crystal jewel.

passages.literal_translation: In the gaps of the mind inclined toward discriminative cognition, whose flow is only the discernment of the distinction between sattva and the conscious subject, other cognitions occur: “I am,” “mine,” “I know,” or “I do not know.” From what? From previous dispositions whose seeds are diminishing. [Sūtra4.28:] Their removal has been explained as with the afflictions. Just as afflictions whose seeds have been burned cannot sprout, so a former disposition, its seed burned by the fire of knowledge, does not produce cognition.

passages.original_text: citeḥ svabuddhisaṃvedanaṃ buddhes tadākārāpattau citipratibimbādhāratayā tadrūpatāpattau satyām.
passages.notes: The opening problem asks how an inactive, unconnected subject could experience mind. This answer does not yet posit Bhikṣu’s second reflection of intellect in consciousness.

passages.literal_translation: Just as clear water into which the moon’s reflection has entered makes the motionless moon appear as if moving, even without action by the moon, so the mind, into which the reflection of consciousness has entered, even without activity by consciousness, through its own activity makes consciousness-power appear active and connected although unconnected. In acquiring the condition of being experienced, it brings about for that [consciousness-power] the condition of being experiencer. This is the meaning of the sūtra.

passages.notes: The source does not deny intrinsic consciousness during dissolution; it distinguishes the liberating endpoint from a state compatible with return.

passages.literal_translation: For consciousness-power is established in its own nature even in the great dissolution. And that is not liberation; hence [the commentator] says “again.”

passages.original_text: yathā ca citi buddheḥ pratibimbam evaṃ buddhāv api citpratibimbaṃ svīkāryam anyathā caitanyasya bhānānupapatteḥ svayaṃ sākṣāt svadarśane karmakartṛvirodhena buddhyārūḍhatayaivātmano ghaṭādivaj jñeyatvābhyupagamāt.
passages.notes: This is Bhikṣu’s solution. Do not attribute the same reasoning to all Advaitins, Trika, or every Yoga commentator.

passages.literal_translation: And just as there is a reflection of intellect in consciousness, so a reflection of consciousness in intellect must also be accepted; otherwise the manifestation of consciousness would be inexplicable. For, owing to the incompatibility of object and agent in directly seeing oneself by oneself, the self is admitted to be knowable, like a pot and the rest, precisely as presented in intellect.

passages.original_text: bimbākāro buddheḥ pariṇāma eva sa ca sākṣibhāsya iti. etena nīrūpatvād buddhipuruṣayor anyonyaṃ pratibimbanaṃ na sambhavatīty apāstam. ubhayatrobhayākārabuddhipariṇāmasyaiva pratibimbaśabdenātra vivakṣitatvāt.

passages.literal_translation: The form of the original is precisely a transformation of intellect, and that is manifested to the witness. By this, [the objection] that mutual reflection of intellect and person is impossible because of lack of form is set aside. For in both cases, precisely the transformation of intellect bearing the respective forms of the two is intended here by the word “reflection.”

passages.notes: Sva/svāmin here describes the instrument’s relation to its experiencer. It is not a recommendation about legal ownership or an assertion that every subject experiences every mind.

passages.literal_translation: Many births of mine and of yours have passed, Arjuna. I know all of them; you do not know them, because your power of knowledge is obstructed by merit, demerit and the like. I, however, being of an eternally pure, awakened and free nature, have an unobstructed power of knowledge; therefore I know. O tormentor of foes.

passages.literal_translation: Although unborn, that is, free from birth; likewise although of imperishable self, whose nature is undiminished knowledge-power; likewise although Lord, disposed to ruling, of beings from Brahmā down to a clump of grass: [I take command of] my own prakṛti, my three-guṇa Vaiṣṇava māyā, under whose sway this entire world exists, deluded by which the world does not know Vāsudeva as its own self. Having taken command of that own prakṛti, having brought it under control, I come forth: I become as though embodied, as though born, through my own māyā—not ultimately as people do.

passages.literal_translation: That birth has the form of māyā, and the action is protecting the good and the rest. Whoever knows this divine—nonordinary, lordly—birth and action of mine truly, just as stated, having abandoned this body, does not attain birth again; he comes to me, he is liberated, Arjuna.

passages.literal_translation: The deluded, undiscriminating people disregard me: they show disrespect, contempt. “Having resorted to a human body” means transacting through a human body. They do not know my higher, excellent nature, the supreme reality of the self, like space, more inward even than space, the great Lord of beings, the great ruler of all beings, their own self. Therefore those pitiable people are injured by their attitude of disregard for me.

passages.literal_translation: [Question:] If the other deities too are precisely you, their devotees also worship you. [Answer:] It is indeed so. [Root:] Even those devoted to other deities who worship endowed with faith worship precisely me, son of Kuntī, but preceded by a wrong procedure. [Śaṅkara:] Those devoted to other deities worship, honor, endowed with faith, an affirmative conviction. They too worship precisely me; avidhi is ignorance, and their worship is preceded by that—this is the meaning. For I am the enjoyer and lord of all sacrifices, Vedic and remembered, as the self of the deities. A sacrifice indeed has me as its master; “I alone am the presiding deity of sacrifice here” was said. But they do not know me truly, as I am. Therefore, having sacrificed with ignorance preceding, they fall away from the fruit of sacrifice.

passages.literal_translation: Others, however, do not accept a body-and-body-possessor relation in the supreme Lord. What [do they hold]? The Lord Vāsudeva who is eternal, pervasive, a mass of being-consciousness-bliss, complete, without guṇas, the supreme self—that himself is his form, not some other [form] constituted of the elements or of māyā.

passages.literal_translation: Having taken my own nature as my basis, remaining precisely in my own nature, I come forth: without any body-and-body-possessor relation, I transact like an embodied one. How, then, is there an appearance of bodiliness in the bodiless mass of being-consciousness-bliss? To this he says, “through my own māyā.” In me, the Lord Vāsudeva, without guṇas, pure, a mass of being-consciousness-bliss, empty of the body-and-body-possessor relation, the appearance in that form is māyā alone—this is the meaning.

They are not to be refuted, by the maxim “one speaking without reasoning is not restrained by us.” If it is possible, let it be just so. What is the use of excessive elaboration? Thus [the discussion] is stopped.

passages.literal_translation: She saw there the whole—the moving and the stationary, space, the directions, the earth-globe with mountains, islands and oceans, with wind, fire, moon and stars; the circle of luminaries, water, radiance, wind and ether, the transformed senses, mind, subtle measures and the three qualities. Seeing this manifold, together with living beings, time, nature, action, dispositions and differences of subtle bodies, in her son’s body, in the opened mouth, and Vraja together with herself, she came to doubt.

passages.literal_translation: When the cowherd woman had thus known the truth, that mighty Lord extended Vaiṣṇava māyā consisting of affection for a son. Immediately losing the memory, she, the cowherd woman, placed her son on her lap and became, as before, one whose heart was filled with increased affection. Hari, whose greatness is sung by the threefold Veda, the Upaniṣads, Sāṅkhya and Yoga, and the Sātvatas, she regarded as her son.

passages.literal_translation: Here itself, in the appearance called Śrī Kṛṣṇa that stills māyā, regarding the whole world clearly seen both outside and within the belly, the māyā-character mentioned before is the falsity of your being delimited by the manifold. That was disclosed—shown—by you to the mother. Thus, “You are only within the world, while the world is outside you”—such is a property of māyā. But in reality, through the intrinsic power difficult to reason out, you are pervasive even with middling size: this is the purport.

passages.original_text: svasya vraje’ntar-bhūtatā-darśanenaiva samaṃ vrajasya svasminn antar-bhūtatāṃ darśayan, tac cāntar-bahir-darśanaṃ kiṃ svapna etad uta deva-māyā [bhā.pu. 10.8.40] ity-ādau śrī-jananyā eva vicāre svāpnikatva-māyikatva-bimba-pratibimbatvānām ayogyatvād ekam evety abhijñāpayan, kiṃ svapna ity-ādāv eva, yaḥ kaścana autpattika ātma-yogaḥ [bhā.pu. 10.8.40] ity anena carama-pakṣāvasitayā durvitarkya-svarūpa-śaktyaiva madhyama-parimāṇa-viśeṣa eva sarva-vyāpako’smīti svayam eva bhagavān jananīṃ prati yugapad ubhayātmakaṃ nija-dharma-viśeṣaṃ darśitavān |
passages.voice: Jīva’s explanatory prose; the first-person “I am” is his formulation of what Bhagavān disclosed, not an additional quotation in the Bhāgavata root.
passages.notes: This argument does not establish that every human or every god has this joint property. The clauses denying dream/illusion/reflection are Jīva’s interpretation of the episode;10.8.40 itself asks questions. An exact mathematical semantics has not yet been derived.

passages.literal_translation: Showing Vraja’s being within himself simultaneously with the display of his own being within Vraja, and making known that this inside-and-outside vision is one and the same—because dreamhood, illusionhood and original-and-reflection status are unsuitable in the mother’s own deliberation beginning “Is this a dream, or divine māyā?”—Bhagavān himself showed the mother his own particular property as having both characters simultaneously: “Precisely as a particular middling magnitude, I am all-pervading,” through the intrinsic power difficult to reason out, settled upon as the last alternative by “some innate power” in that same verse.

passages.literal_translation: That from which the forms of Vraja’s friends and the rest appeared, and by which all of that, at the time of disappearance, remains again as this divine form—that is precisely nondual Brahman: this is the meaning. The purport is that it falls under that characterization through the observed appearance, persistence and disappearance of all worldly and nonworldly things. Consequently, when its being Brahman is established, its pervasiveness too is established: this is the intention.

passages.original_text: vibhūtimadādikaṃ mama tejorūpeṇāṃśena saha bhavatīty uktyā viṣṇvādīnām api bhagavadaṃśayuktatvaṃ pratīyate | teṣām apy etallakṣaṇopetatvāt | tannivṛttyartham āha—viṣṇvādīnīti || […] aṃśayuktatvenoktvā “kalāḥ” ity anena kalā iva kalāḥ | na svarūpatvena | “ete svāṃśakalāḥ” ity anena svarūpāṃśarūpā eva kalāḥ | natu pūrvavad upacāreṇeti ||
passages.voice: Jayatīrtha explaining Madhva; quotation tokens retain the form given in this commentary witness.
passages.notes: Important textual caution: this Madhva/Jayatīrtha witness quotes ete svāṃśakalāḥ. The common Bhāgavata1.3.28 wording is ete cāṃśakalāḥ. Do not silently replace one with the other or present the commentator’s quotation as an independently collated universal root reading. This selection establishes the commentator’s semantic argument, not the stemma of the Bhāgavata verse.

passages.literal_translation: By saying that what possesses splendor and so forth exists together with my portion in the form of radiance, Viṣṇu and the others also appear to be endowed with a portion of Bhagavān, since they too have that characteristic. To remove this [understanding], he says “Viṣṇu and the others.” […] Having spoken of [the first group] as endowed with a portion, by “kalās”: they are kalās as if kalās, not as his own nature. By “these are own-portion kalās”: the kalās have precisely the character of portions of his own nature, not by figurative usage as before.

Although already included by the mention of kings, his repeated mention is to rule out the specific statement that he is a direct avatāra.

[…] [Jayatīrtha:] Forms are Matsya and the rest; acts are creation and the rest; qualities are knowledge and the rest. […] Limbs are hands and the rest. […] The remainder [to be supplied] is: it must be explained precisely in the primary sense.

passages.original_text: sa cāprākṛtarūpatvād arūpaḥ svaguṇātmakam / rūpam asya śiraḥpāṇipādādyātmakam iṣyate // […] prakṛtiśabdo ’nyeṣāmapi tattvānāmupalakṣakaḥ / aprākṛtarūpatvāt / prākṛtarūparahitatvāt / guṇātmakamityukte sattvādīnāṃ pratītiḥ syāt / tannirāsārthaṃ svaśabdaḥ / ye paramātmanaḥ svarūpabhūtā guṇā ānandādyāstadātmakamiti / rūpaśabdena ca śuklādiguṇapratītiḥ syāt / ataḥ śiraḥpāṇīti vivaraṇaṃ kṛtam / ato rūpavāṃśceti śeṣaḥ / […] anityatā janmamaraṇavattā / nāpi saundaryādyabhāva iti ca draṣṭavyam / tathāca tasminbhaktirupapanneti śeṣaḥ /

passages.literal_translation: [Madhva:] And he is formless because his form is not prākṛta. His form, consisting of his own qualities and of head, hands, feet and the rest, is accepted. […] [Jayatīrtha:] The word prakṛti also indicates the other principles. “Because of having non-prākṛta form”: because of being devoid of a prākṛta form. If “consisting of qualities” were said [alone], sattva and the others might be understood; the word “own” removes that. It means consisting of the qualities that are the supreme Self’s own nature, bliss and the rest. And by “form,” the quality white and so forth might be understood; therefore “head, hands” supplies the explanation. Thus, “and he has form” is to be supplied. […] Impermanence is possession of birth and death. Nor is there absence of beauty and the rest: this too should be understood. Therefore devotion to him is coherent: this is to be supplied.

passages.original_text: yatkvacidviruddhamiva pratīyamānamapīśvare taditaratra vā pramāṇasiddhamīśvaraiśvaryavirodhi ca na bhavati / yathāṇutvamahattvayaugapadyādi […] / tatsarvamīśvaraiśvaryabalena ghaṭata ityaṅgīkāryam / natu nirākāryam / yatpunarapramitaṃ tadīśvaraiśvaryāviruddhamapi na kalpanīyam / śaśaviṣāṇādikalpanāpatteḥ /
passages.voice: Jayatīrtha giving the boundary of an appeal to inconceivable power, after an extended objection/reply about the agency and awareness of divine-regulated manifestations.
passages.notes: The omitted example concerns incomplete connected awareness in Arjuna and others, treated earlier in the same debate; its electronic word-junction is not silently emended. The source’s further claim that jīva–God unity undermines sovereignty is a school-internal argument, not a neutral proof against every retyped nondual proposal.

passages.literal_translation: Whatever, even appearing as though contradictory, is established by a means of knowing in the Lord or elsewhere, and is not contrary to the Lord’s sovereignty—for example, simultaneity of smallness and greatness […]—all that is to be accepted as coherent through the Lord’s sovereignty, not rejected. But what is not established by a means of knowing must not be imagined, even if not contrary to that sovereignty, because imagining a hare’s horn and the like would follow.

passages.original_text: aṃśa-śabditatve’pi paro matsyādir na evaṃ jīvavan na bhavati | tatra dṛṣṭāntam āha prakāśeti | yathā tejo’ṃśo raviḥ khadyotaś ca tejaḥ-śabditatve’pi naikarūpya-bhāk | yathā jalāṃśaḥ sudhā-madyādiś ca jala-śabditatve’pi na sāmyaṃ labhate, tadvat ||44||
passages.voice: Baladeva’s own explanation of the sūtra, after raising whether Matsya-type portions differ from jīva-type portions.
passages.notes: The repeated negative na evaṃ…na bhavati is preserved, not silently streamlined. “Portions of radiance/liquid” follows the commentator’s illustrative language and is not a modern physical explanation.

passages.literal_translation: Although called a portion, the supreme Matsya and the rest are not thus—not like the jīva. Here he gives the example “like light.” Just as the sun and a firefly, portions of radiance, do not have the same character despite both being called radiance; and just as nectar, liquor and the rest, portions of liquid, do not attain equality despite both being called liquid—so it is.

passages.original_text: na te jīvavat tato bhidyante, tasyaiva vaidūryādivat tat-tad-bhāvāviṣkārāt | sarva-śakti-vyakty-avyakti-savyapekṣo hi tat-tad-vyapadeśaḥ | yaḥ kṛṣṇaḥ kṛtsna-ṣāḍguṇya-vyañjako’ṃśī, sa evākṛtsna-tad-vyañjako dvy-eka-vyañjako vāṃśaḥ kalā cety ucyate | yathaikaḥ kṛtsna-ṣaṭ-śāstra-pravaktā sarvavid ucyate, sa eva kvacid akṛtsna-tad-vaktā dvy-eka-śāstra-vaktā ca sarvavit-kalpo’lpajñaś ceti |

passages.notes: The six excellences and six teaching disciplines belong to the example’s traditional vocabulary. The paragraph does not by itself assign exact subsets to every avatāra. The source’s spelling savyapekṣa is retained.

passages.literal_translation: They do not differ from him as the jīva does, because that very one reveals the respective forms, like a vaidūrya gem and the like. For the respective designation depends on the manifestation or nonmanifestation of all powers. That very Kṛṣṇa who, displaying all six divine excellences, is the possessor of portions, when not displaying all of them, or displaying two or one, is called a portion or a fraction. Just as one person who teaches all six disciplines is called all-knowing, that very person, somewhere teaching not all of them or teaching two or one, is called almost all-knowing or little-knowing.

passages.original_text: sarvātiśayi-prema-pūrṇa-parikaratva-druhiṇādi-vidvattama-vismāpaka-vaṃśa-mādhurya-sva-paryanta-sarva-vismāpaka-rūpa-mādhurya-niratiśaya-kāruṇyādayo yaśodā-stanandhaye kṛṣṇa eva nityāvirbhūtāḥ santi, na tu matsyāditve satīti tasyaiva tat-tad-bhāvāviṣkārān na matsyāder jīvavat tattvāntaratvaṃ, kintu tad-ātmakatvam eveti ||45||
passages.voice: Baladeva’s own conclusion; excerpt begins inside a longer enumeration whose preceding mention of powers and qualities supplies the grammatical subject.
passages.notes: The Sanskrit is a long descriptive compound; hyphens are editorial aid. The excerpt’s grammatical dependence on the preceding sentence is explicit, not hidden. It does not say that Matsya lacks divine power or is a defective God.

passages.literal_translation: Having associates filled with love surpassing all; the sweetness of the flute that astonishes even the most learned, Brahmā and others; the sweetness of form that astonishes everyone, up to himself; unsurpassed compassion and the rest—these are eternally manifest in Kṛṣṇa alone, the suckling of Yaśodā, not in the condition of Matsya and the rest. Thus, because that very one reveals those respective forms, Matsya and the rest are not another reality as a jīva is, but have precisely his nature.

passages.original_text: naivaṃ matsyādi-rūpasya, kintu deha-sambandha-rāhityaṃ sākṣāt pareśatvaṃ ca tasya śrūyate, ato mahān viśeṣaḥ | […] jīvasyāsantater apūrṇatvād avyatikaraḥ | pūrṇena matsyādinā sāmyaṃ nety arthaḥ | bālāgra-śata-bhāgasya [śve.u. 5.9] ity ādyā śrutir jīvasyāpūrtim āha | pūrṇam adaḥ pūrṇam idam ity ādyā tu matsyādeḥ pūrtim ||47||
passages.voice: Baladeva on two successive sūtras; explicit omission separates46 from47.
passages.notes: Asantati is glossed by the author as apūrṇatva here; do not infer a general spatial definition of every self from the English “nonextension.” The quotations of Upaniṣads are Baladeva’s cited forms, not new independent editions of those Upaniṣads.

passages.literal_translation: It is not so for the Matsya and other forms; rather, absence of association with a body and direct being-the-supreme-Lord are heard of it. Therefore there is a great distinction. […] There is no intermixture, because of the jīva’s nonextension, its incompleteness. The meaning is: there is no equality with complete Matsya and the rest. The revelation beginning “of the hundredth part of a hair-tip” declares the jīva’s incompleteness; that beginning “That is complete, this is complete” declares the completeness of Matsya and the rest.

na ca strīrūpamathavā na puṃrūpamathobhayam //

Through its brilliance their eyes were covered, O lord of the earth. And when the gods, again taking courage, looked, then that very same [luminosity] shone in a female form, divine and captivating.

raktavastraparīdhānāṃ dāḍimīkusumaprabhām //
sarvaśṛṅgāraveṣāḍhyāṃ sarvadevanamaskṛtām /
sarvāśāpūrikāṃ sarvamātaraṃ sarvamohinīm //
prasādasumukhīmambāṃ mandasmitamukhāmbujām /
avyājakaruṇāmūrtiṃ dadṛśuḥ purataḥ surāḥ //

The held IAST and PDF602 read sarvāśāpūrikāṃ; the Satsangdhara electronic text instead reads sarvāśāparipūrikāṃ. See variant register.

passages.original_text:
iti teṣāṃ vacaḥ śrutvā provāca parameśvarī /
mama śaktistu yā gaurī bhaviṣyati himālaye //
śivāya sā pradeyā syāt sā vaḥ kāryaṃ vidhāsyati /
bhaktiryaccaraṇāmbhoje bhūyādyuṣmākamādarāt //
himālayo hi manasā māmupāste 'tibhaktitaḥ /
tatastasya gṛhe janma mama priyakaraṃ matam //
passages.voice: Vyāsa’s speech introduction; then the Goddess herself
passages.notes: At64 yaccaraṇāmbhoje is literally at whose lotus-feet; the antecedent Gaurī is retained here. Satsangdhara’s Hindi paraphrase says my feet, while its Sanskrit preserves yac-. The held IAST places mama before priyakaram in65; the syntactic relation permits “birth in his house is pleasing to me” without silently changing to a possessive “my birth.” The first-person divine referent and Himālaya’s reply still supply the contextual birth identification.

passages.literal_translation: Having heard their words, the supreme Lady said: “My power who is Gaurī will come to be in Himālaya. She should be given to Śiva; she will accomplish your purpose. May your devotion to [her] lotus-feet arise with earnestness. For Himālaya worships me mentally with exceeding devotion. Therefore birth in his house is considered pleasing to me.”

passages.original_text:
adya prapañce kīrtiḥ syājjaganmātā sutābhavat /
aho himālayasyāsya dhanyo 'sau bhāgyavāniti //
yasyāstu jaṭhare santi brahmāṇḍānāṃ ca koṭayaḥ /
saiva yasya sutā jātā ko vā syāttatsamo bhuvi //
passages.notes: This is anticipatory praise after a promise, not a report of a child’s mouth vision. Koṭi is crore/ten million; plural crores should not be silently translated as a mathematical infinity. This is not evidence for all traditions identifying all goddesses or saints identically.

passages.original_text:
antaḥsvānubhavānandā vikalponmuktagocarā |
yāvasthā bharitākārā bhairavī bhairavātmanaḥ || 15 ||

tad vapus tattvato jñeyaṃ vimalaṃ viśvapūraṇam |
evaṃvidhe pare tattve kaḥ pūjyaḥ kaś ca tṛpyati || 16 ||

evaṃvidhā bhairavasya yāvasthā parigīyate |
sā parā pararūpeṇa parā devī prakīrtitā || 17 ||
passages.notes: Do not turn vapus into a claim that every visible deity-image is already this state as delimited image. The question kaḥ pūjyaḥ is a qualification of the ultimate register, not a denial that the text supplies practices. This unit does not establish an avatāra taxonomy or identify human saints.

passages.literal_translation: That state of Bhairava’s self, Bhairavī, whose bliss is one’s own inward experience, whose domain is freed from conceptual construction, whose form is fullness—that is to be known as [his] body in truth, stainless, filling the universe. In such a supreme reality, who is to be worshipped and who is satisfied? That state of Bhairava which is celebrated in this manner—she is the Supreme; in the supreme manner [she] is proclaimed the supreme Goddess.

passages.original_text: অবতার বা অবতারের অংশ, এদের বলে ঈশ্বরকোটি আর সাধারণ লোকদের বলে জীব বা জীবকোটি। যারা জীবকোটি তারা সাধনা করে ঈশ্বরলাভ করতে পারে; তারা সমাধিস্থ হয়ে আর ফেরে না।

passages.notes: Do not reword this as ordinary people cannot attain God: it says they can. Do not generalize the nonreturn claim to every tradition. The classification is M.’s report of Ramakrishna’s teaching, not an independently demonstrable classification of individuals.

passages.romanized_text: Avatār bā avatārer aṃśa, eder bale īśvarakoṭi ār sādhāraṇ lokder bale jīv bā jīvakoṭi. Yārā jīvakoṭi tārā sādhanā kare īśvaralābh karte pāre; tārā samādhistha haye ār phere nā.
passages.literal_translation: An avatāra or a part of an avatāra—these are called īśvarakoṭi; ordinary people are called jīva or jīvakoṭi. Those who are jīvakoṭi can attain God through practice; having entered samādhi they do not return.

authors: Ramakrishna as recorded by Mahendranath Gupta
passages.original_text:
তোমাকে ছুঁলে কি তোমার সব শরীরটা ছুঁতে হবে? যদি গঙ্গাস্নান করি তা হলে হরিদ্বার থেকে গঙ্গাসাগর পর্যন্ত কি ছুঁয়ে যেতে হবে?
[…]
‘আমি’ গেলে কি রইল তা কেউ জানতে পারে না, — মুখে বলতে পারে না। যা আছে তাই আছে! তখন খানিকটা এঁতে প্রকাশ হয়েছে আর বাদবাকিটা ওখানে প্রকাশ হয়েছে, — এ-সব মুখে বলা যায় না।
passages.voice: Ramakrishna’s speech as recorded by M. (Mahendranath Gupta)
passages.notes: Analogy about access does not prove that every bodily part has all properties of the whole, nor that every saint possesses unlimited manifested power. Trailokya’s negative claim must not be quoted as Ramakrishna’s own conclusion. This excerpt omits the immediately preceding idiomatic “ananta ḍhukute cāo keno”; no disputed English rendering of that phrase is used as a premise. The ellipsis omits the intervening maxim and sentence that difference-consciousness lasts while the I remains; it changes neither speaker nor argument. The retained no-one-can-know wording should not be converted into a separate doctrine of annihilation or ignorance in liberation.

passages.romanized_text:
Tomāke chũle ki tomār sab śarīrṭā chũte habe? Yadi gaṅgāsnān kari tā hale haridvār theke gaṅgāsāgar paryanta ki chũye yete habe?
[…]
‘Āmi’ gele ki raila tā keu jānte pāre nā, — mukhe balte pāre nā. Yā āche tāi āche! Takhan khānikṭā ẽte prakāś hayeche ār bādabākiṭā okhāne prakāś hayeche, — e-sab mukhe balā yāy nā.
passages.literal_translation: If I touch you, must I touch your whole body? If I bathe in the Ganges, must I then go on touching from Haridwar to Gangasagar? […] When the I goes, no one can know what remains—cannot say it in words. What is, is! Then, “a portion has manifested in this one and the remainder has manifested over there”—such things cannot be said in words.

authors: Ramakrishna as recorded by Mahendranath Gupta
passages.original_text:
অবতারাদির ‘আমি’ পাতলা ‘আমি’। এ ‘আমি’র ভিতর দিয়ে ঈশ্বরকে সর্বদা দেখা যায়।
[…]
এর মানে, দেহধারণ করলেও তারা সর্বদা যোগেতেই থাকে!
[…]
সমাধিস্থ হলেও আবার নেমে আসতে পারে।
passages.voice: Ramakrishna’s speech as recorded by M. (Mahendranath Gupta)
passages.notes: The passage concerns avatāras and the like, called īśvarakoṭi nearby; it does not make all ordinary personalities or every liberated person equally transparent. The first ellipsis omits the wall/aperture illustration; the second omits its explanation of entering samādhi at will and going and coming through the large aperture. The embodied-yoga and return clauses are included.

passages.romanized_text:
Avatārādir ‘āmi’ pātlā ‘āmi’. E ‘āmi’r bhitar diye īśvarke sarvadā dekhā yāy.
[…]
Er māne, dehadhāraṇ karleo tārā sarvadā yogetei thāke!
[…]
Samādhistha haleo ābār neme āste pāre.
passages.literal_translation: The I of avatāras and the like is a thin I. Through this I, God can always be seen. […] This means that even though they assume a body, they always remain in yoga! […] Even after entering samādhi, they can come down again.

passages.original_text: nanv evaṃ sati yāvatsadadhikaraṇātyantābhāvapratiyogitvaṃ paryavasitam. tathā ca kevalānvayyatyantābhāvapratiyogiṣu avṛttiṣu gaganādiṣu tārkikāṇāṃ siddhasādhanam; yadadhikaraṇaṃ yat sat tanniṣṭhātyantābhāvapratiyogitvaṃ tasya mithyātvam iti vivakṣāyām, adhikaraṇapadenāvṛttinirākaraṇe ’pi saṃyogasambandhena samavāyasambandhena vā yat ghaṭādhikaraṇaṃ samavāyasambandhena saṃyogasambandhena vā ghaṭasya tanniṣṭhātyantābhāvapratiyogitayā sarveṣu vṛttimatsu duruddharaṃ siddhasādhanam. yena sambandhena yad yasyādhikaraṇaṃ tena sambandhena tanniṣṭhātyantābhāvapratiyogitvam iti vivakṣāyām avyāpyavṛttiṣu saṃyogādiṣu siddhasādhanam iti cen na.
passages.voice: Author reports an opponent’s successive objections; closes with his rejection, iti cen na.
passages.notes: Kevalānvayin and avṛtti describe the logicians’ accepted cases in this objection. Do not attribute their whole ontology to Madhusūdana or interpret siddhasādhana as a proof that he accepts ordinary pots as ultimately real.

passages.literal_translation: But, if this is so, [the definition] comes to being the counterpositive of absolute absence whose loci are all existent things. Then, for the logicians, in the case of things such as space which do not occur [in a locus] and are counterpositives of an absolute absence occurring universally, it proves what is already established. If what is intended is “its falsity is being the counterpositive of absolute absence located in that existent thing which is its locus,” then, even though the word “locus” excludes things that do not occur [in a locus], proving what is already established is hard to avoid for all things that do occur [in a locus]: where something is the locus of a pot through contact or inherence, the pot is the counterpositive of absolute absence there through inherence or contact [respectively]. If what is intended is being the counterpositive of absolute absence located there through the very relation through which something is its locus, there is [still] proving what is already established in cases such as contact, which does not occur throughout its locus. If this is the objection: no.

passages.original_text: yadi punaḥ dhvaṃsaprāgabhāvapratiyogitvam ivātyantābhāvapratiyogitvam ākāśādau na syāt; sādhakamānābhāvasya tulyatvāt, ihākāśo nāstīti pratyakṣapratītyasambhavāt, anumāne cānukūlatarkābhāvāt, sāmānyato dṛṣṭamātreṇa dhvaṃsaprāgabhāvapratiyogitvasyāpi siddhiprasaṅgāt, tadvyatirekeṇa kasyacit kāryasyānupapatter abhāvāc ca, evaṃ saṃyogasambandhena ghaṭavati bhūtale samavāyasambandhena ghaṭābhāvasattve mānābhāvāl lāghavena ghaṭātyantābhāvatvenaiva ghaṭasāmānādhikaraṇyavirodhitvakalpanāt sambandhaviśeṣapraveśe ca gauravāt ghaṭasamavāyamātraviṣayatayā pratīter upapatter ādhārādheyabhāvasya pratyakṣasiddhatvena ghaṭasyāvṛttitvaśaṅkānudayād uktayukteś ca na ghaṭāder atyantābhāvasāmānādhikaraṇyam; evaṃ ca saṃyogatadabhāvayor naikādhikaraṇyam; agre vṛkṣaḥ kapisaṃyogī mūle neti pratīter agramūlayor eva saṃyogatadabhāvavattayopapatteḥ, tadā sanmātraniṣṭhātyantābhāvapratiyogitvam eva mithyātvaṃ mantavyam.
passages.voice: Author’s conditional alternative: yadi punaḥ ... tadā ... mantavyam.
passages.notes: Sanmātra is translated cautiously as existent reality as such; it is not the finite set of ordinary objects by stipulation. This passage does not establish a topos, a universal consistency theorem, or the equivalence of every school.

passages.literal_translation: If, however, space and the like were not counterpositives of absolute absence, just as they are not counterpositives of destruction or prior absence—because the lack of establishing evidence is the same; because direct apprehension “space is not here” is impossible; because inference lacks a supporting suppositional argument; because mere inference from general observation would also establish their being counterpositives of destruction and prior absence; and because no effect would be inexplicable without it—and likewise a pot and the like do not share a locus with [their] absolute absence, because there is no evidence for a pot’s absence through inherence on ground that has a pot through contact; because economy warrants positing incompatibility with sharing a locus with a pot simply through being absolute absence of a pot; because introducing a particular relation adds complexity; because the apprehension is explicable as having only the pot’s inherence as its object; because the directly established relation of support and supported prevents a doubt that the pot occurs nowhere; and because of the reasoning already stated; and likewise contact and its absence do not have one locus, since the apprehension “the tree has contact with a monkey at its top, not at its root” is explicable by the top and root themselves having contact and its absence—then falsity is to be understood simply as being the counterpositive of absolute absence located in existent reality as such.

passages.literal_translation: Prior absence is beginningless and has an end: [the absence] of an effect before its production. Destruction has a beginning and no end: [the absence] of an effect after its production. Absolute absence has counterpositiveness delimited by a relation and holds through all three times; for example, “There is no pot on the ground.” Mutual absence has counterpositiveness delimited by the relation of identity; for example, “A pot is not a cloth.”

passages.original_text: atyantābhāvaṃ lakṣayati—traikāliketi. anyonyābhāve ’tivyāptivāraṇāya saṃsargāvacchinneti. dhvaṃsaprāgabhāvayor ativyāptivāraṇāya traikāliketi.
passages.notes: The brief gloss relies on the text’s distinction between relational and identity-delimited absence; a model must state that distinction rather than assume every relation qualifies indiscriminately.

passages.notes: The preceding Devadatta/staff example and compressed introductory compound have documented manuscript/editorial difficulties in this edition; they are not used as unqualified quotation here. The selected contact/inherence and specific/generic examples are legible and correspond to the GRETIL reading, apart from explicit sambandha wording. No claim of a critical edition has been made. The inspected print reads pratiyogika, whereas the held GRETIL transcription reads pratiyogitāka; the quotation and translation here follow the print. passages.literal_translation: Earth and the other successively later principles do not exist without the successively earlier water and so on; therefore they have that much as their nature. For earth would not exist without water, since what flows itself is seen in hardness. Thus, in this order: how [could] the elements [exist] without the subtle elements, those without the unfolding of the senses, and the senses without determination of that particular kind? And all these do not exist deprived of the root cause whose subtle form is connected with them undividedly at their beginning. And how [could] root nature, which is to be experienced, [exist] without an experiencer whose nature is awareness, contracted precisely through sharing in that division of objects of experience, and, through contraction itself, bearing upon itself the net of bonds beginning with time and limited agency? And how [could] undivided awareness have contraction without freedom, the cause of contraction, also designated māyā?

passages.literal_translation: First, it is not, as [on the view] of the Sāṅkhyas, in the form of māyā-made bliss consisting of material sattva, because scripture declares that the Lord cannot be overcome by māyā, and because He is satisfied in Himself. Nor is it, as [on the view] of the advocates of the undifferentiated, in the form of the bliss of the Lord’s intrinsic nature, because an intensification would be inexplicable. Still less, therefore, is it in the form of the individual self’s intrinsic bliss, because that is exceedingly small.

passages.literal_translation: Moreover, in the first two examples there is at least a cause–effect relation, but the words “one” and so forth would still be pointless. This, however, does not fit at all: “Just as, dear one, through one nail-cutter.” For, because the nail-cutter is a final composite, its being a cause of another iron object is itself impossible. How much less could one [be the cause] of all? Thus [Madhva] says “and not.”

passages.literal_translation: Here, by “even ignorant of ordinary [names],” it is indicated that this is relative to results. If [one objects], “Then knowing all through knowing one would be nonprimary”—true. For even the opponent cannot explain it in the primary sense. If that were so, it would follow that a person who had seen clay would have no desire to know particular configurations such as pots and dishes, and the rest.

passages.literal_translation: That [promise] can indeed obtain if the taught [reality] is the material cause, because the effect is nonseparate from it. But its nonseparateness from an efficient cause does not [obtain], because potter and pot are separate. […] And that [knowledge of the effect through knowledge of its material cause] could not obtain if merely efficient causation were accepted. For, when the potter is known, the pot is not [thereby] known.

passages.literal_translation: The principal nature of illumination is reflexive apprehension. Without it, even when its form is differentiated by objects, there is mere clarity, but no non-inertness, because savoring is absent.

passages.literal_translation: Precisely for this reason the self is spoken of, with that intention, as consciousness, the activity of consciousness, and agency in consciousness; for by that it is distinct from the inert.

passages.literal_translation: Through such pure independence, this [subject] does not know an entity established separately; rather, through unrestricted power, it makes its own self, which is not an object of knowledge, an object of knowledge. If it depended upon a distinct knowable, its agency in knowing would wither.

passages.literal_translation: But another [principle], such as māyā or primordial nature, distinct from the illumination of consciousness, is nowhere a cause, since, not appearing, it does not exist. If it appears, because of its identity with illumination, consciousness whose form is illumination alone is the cause, not some such other [principle].

She is not real, not unreal, nor both, because of contradiction; differing from these, a certain existent [power] always is.

Therefore the self always has the form of knowledge and happiness, is real, full and unattached, devoid of the net of duality.

passages.literal_translation: Here the word Śiva denotes the power of knowledge, because the Śiva-principle is the seat of the power of knowledge. The word Śakti too denotes the power of action, because the Śakti-principle is the seat of the power of action; for, in the case of her whose nature is consciousness and bliss, the fittingness of construction everywhere through knowledge and action alone is seen.

passages.romanized_text: Īśvarakoṭir ālādā kathā, — yeman anulom bolum. “Neti” “neti” kare chāde pãuche yakhan dekhe, chādao ye jinise tairī, — ĩṭ, cun, surki, sĩṛio sei jinise tairī. Takhan kakhana chādeo thākte pāre, ābār uṭhā nāmāo karte pāre.
passages.literal_translation: The īśvarakoṭi is a different matter—like going in order and in reverse. Having reached the roof by “not this, not this,” when one sees that the stairs too are made of the same material as the roof—brick, lime and brick-dust—then one may sometimes remain on the roof, and may also go up and down.

passages.original_text: In fact the Inﬁnite does not create, it manifests what is in itself, in its own essence of reality; it is itself that essence of all reality and all realities are powers of that one Reality. The Absolute neither creates nor is created, — in the current sense of making or being made; we can speak of creation only in the sense of the Being becoming in form and movement what it already is in substance and status.

passages.original_text: The opposition we make is mental and conceptual; in reality, the silence of the Spirit and the dynamis of the Spirit are complementary truths and inseparable. The immutable silent Spirit may hold its inﬁnite energy silent and immobile within it, for it is not bound by its own forces, is not their subject or instrument, but it does possess them, does release them, is capable of an eternal and inﬁnite action, does not weary or need to stop, and yet all the time its silent immobility inherent in its action and movement is not for a moment shaken or disturbed or altered by its action and movement;

passages.original_text: Still, when we have found that all things are Sachchidananda, all has not yet been explained. We know the Reality of the universe, we do not yet know the process by which that Reality has turned itself into this phenomenon.

passages.work: The Life Divine I.XIII, The Divine Maya
passages.original_text: And since consciousness is the nature of the original Existence and the essence of its Force, this truth must be a self-perception in Conscious-Being and this determination of the line taken by Force must result from a power of selfdirective knowledge inherent in Consciousness which enables it to guide its own Force inevitably along the logical line of the original self-perception. It is then a self-determining power in universal consciousness, a capacity in self-awareness of inﬁnite existence to perceive a certain Truth in itself and direct its force of creation along the line of that Truth, which has presided over the cosmic manifestation.

passages.original_text: Tellingly, all of the analogies Sri Ramakrishna employs to illustrate the inseparability of Brahman and Śakti also indicate their ontological parity.
passages.voice: Ayon Maharaj / Swami Medhananda, scholarly interpretation

passages.locus: Infinite Paths to Infinite Reality, printed38
passages.original_text: Like fire and its power to burn, Brahman and Śakti mutually entail each other. The bidirectionality of all these analogies clearly rules out an Advaitic interpretation of Sri Ramakrishna’s doctrine of the inseparability of Brahman and Śakti. According to Advaita, Śakti is ontologically dependent on nirguṇa Brahman, but nirguṇa Brahman is not ontologically dependent on Śakti, since Śakti is ultimately unreal. Sri Ramakrishna, by contrast, teaches the mutual ontological dependence of Brahman and Śakti.
passages.voice: Ayon Maharaj / Swami Medhananda, scholarly interpretation

passages.original_text: But when we say, “God said, Let there be Light”, we assume the act of a power of consciousness which determines light out of everything else that is not light; and when we say “and there was Light” we presume a directing faculty, an active power corresponding to the original perceptive power, which brings out the phenomenon and, working out Light according to the line of the original perception, prevents it from being overpowered by all the inﬁnite possibilities that are other than itself.

passages.literal_translation: Some call her austerity; some darkness; others the inert, knowledge, māyā, the principal [principle], primordial nature, power, and the unborn. Those skilled in Śaiva scripture call her reflexive apprehension; others, thinkers on the true meaning of the Veda, call her ignorance.

passages.literal_translation: Even for one who has practiced devotion, if knowledge of me does not arise because of already-begun karma, O mountain, he goes to Maṇidvīpa. Having gone there, he obtains all enjoyments even without desiring them. At their end, knowledge of my consciousness-form would arise fully, O mountain. Through that he would be forever liberated: liberation is through knowledge and not otherwise.
